sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Midland County, Michigan?
sections.html:
Deeds, mortgages and other real property documents for Midland County go to the Register of Deeds at 220 W Ellsworth Street, Midland, MI 48640. The office's phone number is (989) 832-6820, and its fax is (989) 832-6842. Recording hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Anything that arrives after 4:00 p.m. is recorded in order of receipt on the next business day, provided it comes with cash or a check. The vault, where older records are kept, keeps shorter hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The office records warranty deeds, quit claim deeds, land contracts, releases, powers of attorney, liens and plats. It does not prepare legal documents or give legal advice, so a seller who needs a deed drafted should go to an attorney or a title company.

sections.h2: What does Midland County charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
The recording fee is $30.00 for any document, regardless of the number of pages, and the amount includes the state remonumentation and register of deeds automation fees. The county's fee sheet adds a few other line items that sellers run into.

Midland County Register of Deeds fee sheet
ItemAmount
Recording any document, any length$30.00
Document assigning or discharging more than one instrument$3.00 per instrument, added to the $30.00
Tax certificate from the County Treasurer$5.00 for up to 5 legal descriptions, $1.00 for each more
Copy of a recorded document$1.00 per page
Certified copy$5.00 plus $1.00 per page

The office takes cash, a check payable to Register of Deeds, or a card at the counter, with a handling charge from the card processor that the office puts at about $1.50. It also accepts e-recording from qualified submitters, which is how many title companies send closing documents. Documents that need a raised court seal or a death certificate cannot be e-recorded.

sections.h2: Does a Midland County deed need a tax certificate?
sections.html:
Yes for several deed types. The county's recording page says a tax certificate must be obtained from the County Treasurer's Office before recording any of these:

  • A warranty deed or any deed that contains a covenant of warranty.
  • A land contract.
  • An assignment of a land contract with a warranty clause.
  • A master deed for a site condominium.

Order the certificate before closing day, since the deed cannot go on record without it. A quit claim deed does not appear on that list. A seller who wants to check whether property taxes are current can use the county's online property and tax lookup, which the county says shows the same information as the treasurer's counter.

sections.h2: How is transfer tax figured in Midland County?
sections.html:
The county's chart applies $3.75 per $500 for the state and $0.55 per $500 for the county, for $4.30 per $500 combined. On a $100,000 price the chart lands at $750 state, $110 county and $860 total. Payment is required whenever the value of the real estate is $100 or more, with exemptions for situations such as the transfers described in the state and county exemption sheets that the office links.

The price paid can be left off the deed if a Real Estate Transfer Tax Valuation Affidavit accompanies it. Separately, the Property Transfer Affidavit goes to the assessor of the City of Midland or whichever township holds the parcel, and the buyer files it within 45 days of the transfer.

sections.h2: What should sellers know about the county's land records and geography?
sections.html:
Midland County was organized in 1855, and the register's indexes begin that year. Records from 1968 onward are scanned and indexed in the computer system, images are online back to 1950, and older records are held in books and microfilm. Search runs through the Fidlar-hosted Tapestry EON and Laredo tools, and the public can copy any recorded document.

The county covers about 517 square miles of land, according to the Census Bureau, and has two incorporated cities: Midland, the county seat, and Coleman. The Tittabawassee River runs through Edenville Township and past the village of Sanford, and in May 2020 the failure of the Edenville and Sanford dams forced evacuations in parts of the city of Midland and several townships. A seller in a river area should have flood and drainage questions answered in writing before listing. Dow Chemical was founded in the city of Midland in 1890, according to the county's history.

Utilities shape what a buyer asks about. The city of Midland supplies water and sewer to city residents and some adjoining townships, while parcels in unincorporated areas without municipal water depend on private wells and septic systems. The county's winters are cold and snowy, with January highs around freezing, and the summers are hot and rainy. A seller outside the city limits should expect questions about the well, the septic system and the basement, and should gather any records before listing.

sections.h2: What is the order of steps for a Midland County sale?
sections.html:
The sequence below follows the county's recording rules and the state statutes, and a title company usually handles most of it.

  • Order a tax certificate from the County Treasurer if the deed carries a warranty clause.
  • Sign the deed before a notary. The register's office does not notarize, but the County Clerk next door does for a fee.
  • Pay state and county transfer tax to the county treasurer within 15 days after the deed is delivered, as MCL 207.523(3) requires.
  • Record the deed with the $30.00 fee, ideally before 4:00 p.m. so it posts that business day.
  • The buyer files the Property Transfer Affidavit with the City of Midland or the township assessor within 45 days.

The register also reports recorded deeds to the local assessor at least once a month under MCL 211.27a(10), so the assessor sees each recorded sale.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show about Midland County homes?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau estimates 83,754 residents and 37,723 housing units for 2025. Of the occupied homes, 78.1 percent are owner-occupied, the median owner-occupied value for 2020 to 2024 is $195,400, and median gross rent is $1,016. Median household income is $77,705, 36.6 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree, and the county issued 128 building permits in 2025.

About 22 percent of occupied homes are rented, households average 2.36 people, and 90.0 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so most owners stay put. Mean travel time to work is 23.7 minutes. The population has risen only 0.3 percent since the April 2020 base, which is a slow-moving market for a seller to read.

faqs.q: Where is the Midland County Register of Deeds?
faqs.a: It is at 220 W Ellsworth Street, Midland, MI 48640, and the phone number is (989) 832-6820. Recording hours are 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday through Friday.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Midland County?
faqs.a: The recording fee is $30.00 for any document, no matter how many pages. A tax certificate for a warranty deed costs $5.00 for up to five legal descriptions.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a deed in Midland County?
faqs.a: Yes, for qualified submitters, including documents that need tax certification. Documents that require a raised court seal or a death certificate cannot be e-recorded.

faqs.q: Does the register of deeds notarize or prepare documents?
faqs.a: No. The office does not prepare legal documents, and it does not notarize the papers it records. The County Clerk's office next door in the County Services Building has a notary for a small fee.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer tax on a $100,000 sale in Midland County?
faqs.a: It is $860, made up of $750 state tax and $110 county tax, according to the county's transfer tax chart.
